params.question: In public health, a group can be called a 'community' only if its members live in the same geographic area, such as a village or urban slum.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite — geography is only one basis for a community. A factory workforce, a tribal cluster, or a school population also count as communities because they share health risks and can be reached through collective action, even without sharing a residence.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — a community is defined by any shared characteristic (geography, culture, occupation, or interest) combined with shared health risks and the ability to be reached through collective action. A factory workforce or a school population qualifies just as a village does.

params.question: A medical officer has identified three community health problems and wants to objectively compare them by scoring the magnitude of each problem, its severity, and the effectiveness of the available intervention, to decide which to tackle first. Which tool should she use?

answers.text: PEARL criteria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PEARL checks whether an intervention is feasible at all — propriety, economics, acceptability, resources, and legality — it does not produce a comparative numerical score.

answers.text: Hanlon's Basic Priority Rating System

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — Hanlon's system multiplies magnitude, severity, and the effectiveness of the intervention to generate a score, allowing problems to be ranked against each other.

answers.text: Kark and Cassel's COPC framework

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This framework describes the process of community-oriented primary care and diagnosis, not a scoring method for prioritising already-identified problems.

answers.text: SWOT analysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SWOT analysis is a general strategic-planning tool; it is not the epidemiological prioritisation method used in community health action planning.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: PEARL is a feasibility gate (yes/no on each criterion), while Hanlon's Basic Priority Rating System is the scoring formula used to rank problems against each other.
Right — Hanlon's formula (magnitude × severity × effectiveness) is the tool built specifically to rank competing community health problems.

params.question: Which of the following best explains why India's primary health care system is described as a 'hybrid' model?

answers.text: National vertical programmes like the TB Programme and RCH Programme function like Selective PHC, while the three-tier PHC infrastructure staffed by ASHAs, ANMs, and multipurpose workers delivers the broader comprehensive vision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — India runs high-impact vertical programmes alongside comprehensive PHC infrastructure, combining both approaches rather than choosing one.

answers.text: India abandoned comprehensive PHC entirely in favour of the GOBI-FFF strategy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: India did not abandon comprehensive PHC — the three-tier Sub-Centre/PHC/CHC structure with ASHAs and ANMs continues to deliver the full comprehensive vision alongside vertical programmes.

answers.text: It combines only public and private hospitals to widen access

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The public-private mix is not what the term 'hybrid' refers to here — it refers to combining Selective PHC-style vertical programmes with comprehensive PHC infrastructure.

answers.text: It applies all eight comprehensive PHC elements through vertical programmes alone, without any general infrastructure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes neither approach correctly — vertical programmes are selective in focus, and general infrastructure (Sub-Centres, PHCs, CHCs) is what carries the comprehensive elements.

overallFeedback.feedback: The hybrid lies in combining two things: vertical programmes (TB, UIP, RCH) that behave like Selective PHC, and the general three-tier PHC infrastructure that delivers comprehensive care.
Exactly — India layers Selective PHC-style vertical programmes on top of a comprehensive three-tier PHC infrastructure.

interactions.label: A district reports 92% full immunisation coverage but has shown no improvement i

params.question: A district reports 92% full immunisation coverage but has shown no improvement in its infant mortality rate over several years. What does this pattern most likely indicate?

answers.text: A coverage gap in immunisation services

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Coverage is already high at 92%, so a coverage gap is not the issue here — the process indicator is strong.

answers.text: A quality problem in service delivery or unaddressed determinants such as nutrition and sanitation, despite good process performance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — strong process numbers alongside poor outcomes point to a quality problem in how services are delivered, or to other unaddressed determinants of child survival.

answers.text: Both indicators are measuring the same thing and are therefore redundant

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Process and outcome indicators measure different things — one measures system effort, the other measures results — so they are not redundant even when they diverge.

answers.text: The district needs no further nutrition or sanitation interventions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The opposite is more likely true: since immunisation effort alone has not moved the outcome, nutrition, sanitation, or care-quality gaps probably still need attention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the rule: strong process numbers with poor outcomes point to a quality problem, while weak process numbers immediately flag a coverage gap.
Right — when process indicators are strong but outcomes lag, the problem usually lies in the quality of care or in determinants beyond the single intervention being measured.

interactions.label: Why is the ASHA referred to as a community health 'activist' rather than a medic

params.question: Why is the ASHA referred to as a community health 'activist' rather than a medical or clinical worker?

answers.text: Because she completes an 18-month diploma in nursing and midwifery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the ANM, who is a salaried clinical worker with an 18-month diploma — not the ASHA.

answers.text: Because her main role is generating community demand for health services through incentive-based tasks, not delivering clinical care

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — the ASHA is unsalaried and works on incentives for tasks like institutional delivery referrals and ANC registration; her job is mobilising the community, while the ANM delivers the clinical care.

answers.text: Because she manages vector control and environmental sanitation at the Sub-Centre

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the Male Health Worker's role, not the ASHA's — the ASHA's focus is household-level demand generation.

answers.text: Because she supervises the ANM at the Sub-Centre

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The reporting relationship runs the other way — the ASHA reports to the ANM and the PHC medical officer, and the ANM supervises the ASHAs in her area.

overallFeedback.feedback: Keep the roles distinct: the ASHA mobilises the household and earns incentives for specific tasks, the ANM delivers salaried clinical care from the Sub-Centre and supervises ASHAs, and the Male Health Worker handles environmental health.
Exactly — the ASHA's incentive-based, community-mobilising role is what earns her the title 'activist' rather than 'health worker.'

params.question: A patient in a remote district skips the local Community Health Centre (CHC) and instead travels 90 km to a district hospital, incurring heavy out-of-pocket expenses. Which combination of the three dimensions of healthcare inaccessibility best explains this behaviour?

answers.text: Geographic inaccessibility alone — the CHC is simply too far away

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The patient is bypassing a nearby CHC, not lacking access to one — the driving factor here is not distance to the CHC itself.

answers.text: Quality inaccessibility at the CHC (missing specialists) drives the patient to bypass it, which in turn produces financial inaccessibility from the resulting travel and out-of-pocket costs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — the 30% specialist shortfall at CHCs pushes patients to bypass them for district hospitals or private care, and that bypass is precisely what generates the catastrophic out-of-pocket costs described as India's biggest health financing failure.

answers.text: Financial inaccessibility alone, since public facilities are always free of cost

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Public facilities are not the source of the cost here — the expense arises because the patient is bypassing the public CHC for a district hospital or private care due to a quality gap.

answers.text: The three dimensions are independent of one another and this reflects personal preference only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The three dimensions compound each other — a quality gap at one tier of the system pushes patients further afield, which then creates a financial burden. They do not act in isolation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Trace the chain: a quality shortfall (missing specialists at the CHC) causes patients to bypass the nearest facility, and that bypass is what creates the financial burden of travelling further for care.
Right — quality gaps (missing CHC specialists) and financial gaps (out-of-pocket bypass costs) are linked, not separate problems.
